Cambridge: Open Book Publishers (World Oral Literature Series 3), 296 pp. DOI 10.11647/OBP.0033. Ch. VI 'Stories on Demand: A Performance Session Among the Bwile', pp. 211-246.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnography of a 1989 storytelling session at Chiengi (Chief Puta); the Bwile narratives are printed in English translation only, with no Bwile text, no phonology, no remark on tone, stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text for tone/stress/accent/syllable/penult returns only non-linguistic uses). The six linked video DOIs 10.11647/obp.0033.06/bwile1-6 are the only Bwile-language audio-visual material found.

sources.citation: Royal Museum for Central Africa (RMCA/MRAC), Tervuren. 'Lexico' lexicostatistic database, language sheet Bantu M401 Bwile: 92-item basic vocabulary, every entry sourced 'lexico : Crine 1967' (field list by [Fernand] Crine, 1967); data collected for Bastin, Y., A. Coupez & M. Mann. 1999. Continuity and Divergence in the Bantu Languages: perspectives from a lexicostatistic study (Annales Sciences humaines 162). Tervuren: MRAC. PDF export (FileMaker, 2008-03-14), 6 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No prose at all. The 92 citation forms are fully TONE-MARKED (grave = low, acute = high, circumflex = falling on long/contracted vowels), e.g. kùlóléshà 'voir', kátápà 'vert', mùkúlú 'grand', kùfîtà 'noir', múlópà 'sang', kû-súmà 'mordre', mwânìké 'petit', tândà 'étoile'. This is first-hand evidence that Bwile was recorded in 1967 as a language with lexical H/L tone (Bemba-type infinitives kù-/kú- with stem tone contrasts), but it is tone MARKING in a wordlist, not a statement about tone or stress — 'wordlist-only' data.

sources.citation: van Bulck, Gaston. 1954. Liste des langues et dialectes du Congo belge. Bulletin des Séances de l'Institut Royal Colonial Belge / Mededelingen der Zittingen 25(1): 258 ff. (séance du 15 février 1954). Bruxelles: IRCB.

sources.note: no phonology content — a bare hierarchical list of languages and dialects; kiBwile is classed as a dialect of kiBeemba (Bemba), nothing on its sounds, tone or stress.

sources.citation: Whiteley, Wilfred H. (with B. Stefaniszyn). 1950 [1951]. Bemba and Related Peoples of Northern Rhodesia (Ethnographic Survey of Africa, East Central Africa, Part II). London: International African Institute. Read as reproduced in Human Relations Area Files, file FQ5 'Bemba' (microfiche; archive.org item micro_IA41160207_0002, categories 101 and 105).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology content. The only language paragraph ('General cultural characteristics') says the languages of the whole group are 'closely similar, so much so that the whole group.. has been loosely termed "Bemba-speaking"', summarises Guthrie 1948 (Bemba with Aushi; Tabwa with Shila), and adds: 'No mention is made of the languages spoken by other small groups closely related to the Bemba, such as Chishinga, Mukulu, Ngumbu, Kawendi, and Bwile.' — an explicit 1950 statement that nothing was known about Bwile speech.
